vignette:
Kwame Mensah is a 78-year-old retired-schoolteacher-turned-librarian who still works three afternoons a week at a neighborhood branch library, shelving returns and helping children find books. He had been at a downtown civic festival two years ago when a bomb detonated near the food stalls. What remains with him is not a blurred impression but a scene he can recount with painful precision: the crack of the blast, the metal barricade twisting, a child's shoe in the street, people shoving past an older woman who had fallen. What grips him most, even now, is the sense that in those seconds ordinary rules vanished. He cannot think about the event without returning to the sight of people trampling one another to get away, and that moral rupture has become part of what makes certain moments in the present feel intolerable.

Since then, his memory of the bombing has stayed vivid and cinematic, as if a strip of film starts running in his mind with no warning. He describes it as the whole scene coming back at once, not in fragments but in full detail. At the library, if patrons begin arguing loudly at the circulation desk, or if he overhears conversations about terrorism, public violence, or even "how people only care about themselves," the memory arrives immediately and completely. Around the anniversary each year, he begins bracing days in advance, because he knows the date itself can pull the scene closer. In this way, the memory has made particular triggers sharply potent: talk about human cruelty, reminders of the date, and examples of people behaving badly all feel as if they open a trapdoor beneath him.

He has organized his life around staying away from those moments. He no longer goes with his wife to church anniversary banquets, street fairs, or crowded holiday events. At work he asks coworkers to cover children's programming days when the library is busiest, and he times his shelving for the quietest hours so he can avoid clusters of people gathering near the front desk. If a patron starts discussing an attack they saw on the news, or complains bitterly about how selfish people have become, Kwame finds a reason to retreat to the stacks. He has also begun turning down things that might lift his mood-family cookouts, his granddaughter's music recital, even small outings his wife plans-because feeling hopeful or light seems dangerous to him, too easily broken. The same vivid memory that ambushes him has taught him to pull back from crowds, difficult conversations, and even pleasure, in the belief that distance is the only way to stay steady.

Over the months, retreating has not quieted the bombing so much as given it more room. When Kwame withdraws from family gatherings or sits alone in the staff room instead of joining colleagues, he often drifts off into an inward, almost dreamlike state, staring past the present until the old scene begins replaying again. Emptying his days of bustle and of joy has left long stretches in which the film can run uninterrupted. His wife has noticed that after he refuses an outing and remains home in his chair, he is often less present by evening, as though he has traveled somewhere she cannot reach. The more he escapes into his own mind and narrows his world, the more available the memory becomes.

Those same habits have also made his triggers harder to avoid, not easier. Because he no longer tolerates busy public places, even ordinary disorder now stands out sharply: a rude exchange in the library, teenagers pushing past one another at the computer station, a heated discussion in the break room. His avoidance has thinned his life down to a few settings, and within them he scans quickly for signs of people behaving badly or for talk that might turn toward violence. The anniversary has become especially charged because his family now tiptoes around it, which only leaves the date looming larger in the house. What he tries not to encounter has become easier to notice.

By the time he came for help, the pattern had tightened around both work and home. His wife told him she felt she was losing him to silence and distance, and the library director gently raised concerns after he twice left the front desk abruptly when patrons began discussing an overseas bombing. Kwame himself was shaken by how quickly the memory still takes him over, and by how small he has let his life become. He says he wants, at his age, to sit at his granddaughter's recital and walk through a crowded room without feeling the film start again. What frightens him most is the possibility that if he lets himself rejoin the world-even for something good-one careless conversation, one act of selfishness, or one date on the calendar will pull him straight back to that day.
